I am an economic geographer and post-doctoral researcher working at the intersection 
of urban economics, institutional history, and satellite remote sensing.

I grew up in India, and questions about cities — why some grow and others don't, 
who gets to own a home, and how the past casts long shadows on the present — have 
shaped my research from the beginning. My PhD at LSE's Department of Geography and 
Environment examined how colonial institutions and contemporary financial markets 
together produce persistent patterns of spatial inequality and urban development in 
India. One strand traced how the opium trade financed early capital accumulation and 
shaped which cities grew. Another used the rollout of housing finance institutions 
in the 1990s to study how mortgage access changed tenure choice across social groups. 
A third examined how colonial land tenure arrangements in Mumbai continue to constrain 
formal residential construction today.

I am currently a Post-Doctoral Research Associate at [Imago](https://imago.liverpool.ac.uk), 
the UKRI Imagery Data Service at the University of Liverpool. Here, I work on 
the Sun Probability Framework — a satellite data project that uses high-resolution Sentinel-2 cloud masks to make a measure of sunlight exposure across Great Britain. More broadly, I am excited about bringing satellite-derived environmental data to bear on questions about 
equity, development, and housing in the Global South, where administrative data is 
often scarce or unreliable.

Before my PhD, I worked at the Centre for Social and Economic Policy (formerly 
Brookings Institution India Center) in New Delhi, where I worked on housing, property rights, and urban infrastructure. I hold a Master's degree in Urban Policy and Governance from the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, Mumbai, and an undergraduate degree in Economics from the University of Delhi.

Outside research, I mentor young women from South Asia who are pursuing careers in economics and policy.
